Suliga , Glennys R. Farrar View a PDF of the paper titled Lightest and heaviest nuclei as keys to the origin of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays, by Anna M. Suliga and Glennys R. Farrar View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: The origin of ultrahigh energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has been a long-standing mystery. A unique feature of UHECRs originating in binary neutron star mergers (BNSMs) is two distinct populations of light elements -- those directly accelerated in the jets, and photo-disintegration products of massive nuclei accelerated in the bulk outflow. We show that Pierre Auger Observatory spectrum and composition data confirm the existence of the predicted two populations at $\geq \!7.2\sigma$ significance, having rigidity ($R\equiv E/Ze$) cutoffs agreeing with prior estimates. The data also favor 5-10% of UHECRs originating as r-process nuclei, a signature of a BNSM origin. Our results provide strong evidence that UHECRs are produced by merging neutron stars, and show how UHECRs and UHE-neutrinos elucidate otherwise inaccessible aspects of neutron star mergers. A key technique for the study of dark matter is weak gravitational lensing: a phenomenon where light from distant galaxies is sheared as it passes through the gravitational field of a massive object, like a galaxy cluster. This shear, which manifests as a slight (weak) distortion of shapes over thousands of galaxies, allows astrophysicists to infer the distribution of total matter, including both luminous and dark matter. pages.text: [DRAFT] Policy on the use of AI tools in W3C Standardization work Skip to content [DRAFT] Policy on the use of AI tools in W3C Standardization work Status: This is a draft document for discussion and review; it is not (yet) a W3C policy. Feedback welcome through GitHub in the TPAC 2026 breakout session proposal . Purpose This policy sets expectations and requirements for any use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for standards work at W3C. It builds on the Use of Large Language Models in Standards Work document published by W3C’s Advisory Board. In general, a variety of tools are used in W3C to help with the development of technical specifications and best practices, including for authoring, versioning, validation, analysis, cross-linking, and automation. These tools are valued when they improve collaboration. Due to their ability to generate content at will, AI tools may hinder collaboration when their usage is unsanctioned or without guardrails. This policy is based upon the principle that every W3C contribution must be attributable to a human contributor who has reviewed and approved its content before publication, understands its substance, and accepts responsibility for its relevance, meaningfulness, correctness, quality, security, scope, provenance, and compliance with other applicable W3C policies . AI tools may be used to assist with a contribution, but may not be treated as contributors or act as unsupervised participants in W3C work. These are special-cased by the Python compiler to allow the use of new Python features in modules containing the future statement before the release in which the feature becomes standard. While these future statements are given additional special meaning by the Python compiler, they are still executed like any other import statement and the __future__ exists and is handled by the import system the same way any other Python module would be. This design serves three purposes: To avoid confusing existing tools that analyze import statements and expect to find the modules they’re importing. To document when incompatible changes were introduced, and when they will be — or were — made mandatory. This is a form of executable documentation, and can be inspected programmatically via importing __future__ and examining its contents. To ensure that future statements run under releases prior to Python 2.1 at least yield runtime exceptions (the import of __future__ will fail, because there was no module of that name prior to 2.1). The Mystic Link Trail is a conceptual effort to link together various green spaces to form a route from Ward Reservation in Andover, MA, US down to Boston, ending at the wharf where the Constitution is docked. See the main website for all the details. In its present form, it’s a little over 32 miles long. We have a relation defined in Open Streetmap to gather all the relevant ways, and a downloadable GPX file with mile markers for easy on-device following. Note that there are some areas where bicycles are not permitted, so there will be an alternate relation so riders can bypass some minor sections. Polyscias gymnocarpa `ohe`ohe View Profile FWS Focus overview characteristics geography timeline information & media contact Overview Polyscias gymnocarpa, a member of the Araliaceae (ginseng) family, is a tree 2.5 to 10 m (8 to 33 ft) tall, either hairless or with fuzzy, short-lived hairs on young leaves and flower clusters. The leaves are 30 to 55 cm (12 to 22 in) long with 7 to 21 leathery, oval to elliptic leaflets per leaf. Each leaflet is 7 to 18 cm (2.8 to 7.1 in) long and 3 to 8 cm (1.2 to 3.1 in) wide and is folded upward along the midvein. The flowers are usually arranged in threes or in an umbrella-shaped arrangement. Petals are 4 to 8 mm (0.2 to 0.3 in) long and usually number 5 or 6 per flower; with an equal number of stamens. The ovary has 3 or 4 sections and appears placed atop the receptacle (base of the flower) in a superior position, due to the expansion of the ovary disk (outgrowth of the receptacle) and the reduction of the hypanthium (basal portion of the flower). Fruits are purplish, oval or top-shaded drupes, 6 to 12 mm (0.2 to 0.5 in) long, that enclose a papery endocarp and single seeds. It had devastating impacts on cotton production, a highly child-labor-intensive crop. This study examines how the arrival of the boll weevil and the subsequent reductions in child labor affect later-life mortality outcomes. Using Social Security Administration death records linked with the 1940 census, we document that the staggered spread of the boll weevil improved the longevity of exposed male children. Full exposure to the boll weevil is associated with an intent-to-treat effect of 1-3 months of higher longevity. pages.text: A bold plan to save Africa’s shrinking giraffe herds | National Geographic By Joshua Foer Photographs by Ami Vitale 25 min read This story appears in the October 2019 issue of National Geographic magazine. Of all the large African mammals that wildlife veterinarian Pete Morkel has had to capture over his career—lions, forest elephants, white rhinos— giraffes are the most stressful. “With other animals, you’re trying to give just enough anesthetic to immobilize them, but with a giraffe, we use a total overdose to chemically knock them off their feet,” the sun-leathered 59-year-old tells me as I stalk him stalking a two-year-old female giraffe somewhere in the Nigerien bush, about 60 miles east of Niamey, Niger’s capital. He is wearing a camo hat and a pair of torn, purple-checkered boxers that he’s been wearing as shorts for the past several days. ( Giraffes Seen Feasting on Skeleton—Here's Why) Morkel has loaded his dart gun with a dose of etorphine, an opioid about 6,000 times more powerful than morphine. Once it penetrates the giraffe’s skin, he and his team will have just minutes to chase down the animal, tackle her, and inject her neck with an antidote to keep her from dying. If she can be successfully captured and survive a 500-mile translocation across Niger, she’ll become one of eight founding “Adams” and “Eves” of a new population of one of the world’s rarest wild mammals. pages.text: A Brief History of Banned Books in America Skip to main content There's More to That A Smithsonian magazine special report The New English Canaan by Thomas Morton criticized the Puritan government in the Massachusetts Bay Colony. Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz The American Library Association reports that 2022 saw more attempts to have books removed from schools and public libraries than in any prior year this century—indeed, it documented nearly twice as many attempted bans in 2022 than in 2021. Notably, the common thread in these aggressive efforts is the subject that binds the most-challenged titles: Most of them address themes of LGBT+ identity or gender expression. On our latest episode of the Smithsonian magazine podcast “There’s More to That,” I talk with journalist Colleen Connolly about Thomas Morton’s New English Canaan , the first book ever to be suppressed in North America. What did the Puritans find so threatening about it, and how has this book echoed through subsequent centuries? Then I’m joined by Carla Hayden, the librarian of Congress, for a wide-ranging conversation about the history of book bans in the United States, how a resurgent wave of book bans in many states differs from those of prior eras and why organized attempts to prevent specific people from reading specific books usually fail. Like clockwork about once a month, his Korean mother-in-law comes to his home and whips it up, unasked, alongside a feast of dumplings called mandu , rice, and two-to-three containers of homemade kimchi . “I don’t want her to come over and cook, but that’s what she wants to do!” says the James Beard Award-winning chef and Momofuku alum, just the slightest bit exasperated. pages.text: A Brief History of Haiti's Cherished Soup Joumou Skip to main content Soup joumou is a savory, orange-tinted soup that typically consists of calabaza squash, beef, noodles, carrots, cabbage, various other vegetables and fresh herbs and spices. Courtesy of Nadege Fleurimond Growing up as a Haitian American, January 1 has always been more than just the start of the new year for me. As a child, waking up on New Year’s Day, I practically floated through the air to the aromas of soup joumou , or Haitian pumpkin soup, resting in one of the decorative bowls my mother reserved for the annual tradition. Every New Year’s Day, Haitians around the world consume soup joumou as a way to commemorate Haitian Independence Day. On January 1, 1804, Haitians declared independence from French colonial rule following the Haitian Revolution that began in 1791. Soup joumou is a savory, orange-tinted soup that typically consists of calabaza squash—a pumpkin-like squash native to the Caribbean—that’s cooked and blended as the soup’s base. Tim Whitmarsh—a classicist at the University of Cambridge and author of magisterial books about empire, the early novel and more—offers a compelling answer in his new book, Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire and the Making of Christianity. To wit, Christianity took much of its shape from the cult of Augustus, first emperor of Rome. The Augustan age saw a unique revolution that redefined authority, space and literature, remaking both the inner world and the outer. Augustus drew on centuries-old Roman prophecies to cast himself as the promised one . According to his propaganda, Italy experienced auguries and miracles at Augustus’ nativity; Augustus was declared a descendant of Rome’s mythical founder, Aeneas, and therefore of the gods, and he promised to renew Roman liberty from the decadence of the late Republic. As Whitmarsh writes: “The new world was presented as the fulfillment of all the best ideals of the old.” Just so, Jesus’s birth was claimed as the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies about a coming emissary of God on Earth, and this novel form of monotheism was simultaneously cast as the fruition of the Hebrew faith. pages.text: A Famous Portrait of Anne Boleyn Hides a Strange Secret | National Geographic Premium HISTORY & CULTURE A Famous Portrait of Anne Boleyn Hides a Strange Secret A scientific analysis of the Hever Rose portrait has revealed a curious choice by its artist—one that hints at a vicious battle over the legitimacy of Boleyn's daughter, Queen Elizabeth I. Anne Boleyn's detractors accused her of immorality and hinted that she had the features of a witch. The Hever Rose portrait, pictured here, may have been created to refute those claims. Pictorial Press Ltd/Alamy By Kelly Faircloth Published November 13, 2026 It’s one of the most famous images of one of history’s most infamous women: The “Hever Rose” portrait of Anne Boleyn depicts the controversial figure for whom England’s King Henry VIII broke with Papal Rome. Pale against a dark background and her own dark attire, Boleyn’s face is poised, almost grave; her sleek hair is half-covered by one of her iconic French hoods and her “B” pendant gleams at her neck. She holds a rose,an important Tudor emblem, delicately at her breast. In fact, she’s holding the rose a bit oddly, clasped between thumb and forefinger. All ten fingers are immediately visible against the rich fabric of her gown. It’s not how most people would instinctively hold a rose. As it turns out, there may be a reason for the prominence of her hands in the painting—one that speaks to rumors which dogged Boleyn even after her death, and which threatened the legitimacy of her daughter, Queen Elizabeth I. Butcher shops, medicine stores and sugar-cane juice stalls crowd the narrow streets. Power lines tangle overhead. For many who live here, access to safe water remains a particular challenge. Published November 5, 2009 • 3 min read Location: Texas Established: June 12, 1944 Size: 801,163 acres Chihuahuan Desert vegetation—bunchgrasses, creosote bushes, cactuses, lechuguillas, yuccas, sotols, and more—covers most of the terrain. But the Rio Grande and its lush floodplains and steep, narrow canyons form almost a park of their own. So do the Chisos Mountains; up to 20 degrees cooler than the desert floor, they harbor pine, juniper, and oak, as well as deer, mountain lions, bears, and other wildlife. A heavy rain transforms the desert: Normally dry creek beds roar with water, and seeds long dormant burst into fields of wildflowers. The rocks of Big Bend are a complex lot. Two seas, one after another, flowed and subsided in the region hundreds of millions of years ago, leaving thick deposits of limestone and shale. The present mountains, except the Chisos, uplifted along with the Rockies, roughly 75 million years ago. Around the same time, a 40-mile-wide trough—most of the present-day park—sank along fault lines, leaving the cliffs of Santa Elena Canyon to the west and the Sierra del Carmen to the east rising 1,500 feet and more above the desert floor. pages.text: A historic guide to San Marino | National Geographic Paid content for Visit San Marino By Julia Buckley Published June 4, 2026 Perched on the aptly named Monte Titano, or Mount Titan, the landlocked city-state of San Marino enjoys spectacular views. Everywhere you look, there’s 360-degree panoramas of the rolling hills of Emilia-Romagna and the Marche regions, cascading down to the Adriatic Sea. While the ravishing landscapes of this part of the peninsula haven’t changed, history has waged major upheaval: over the centuries, the surrounding regions have gone from independent states to occupied territories and, finally, a unified Italy. San Marino however, sat on its eyrie, has remained above the fray — one of Europe’s oldest (and smallest) republics, its borders haven’t changed since 1463. Visitors often include a visit to San Marino as part of a wider trip to Italy, but while curiosity is often what lures people up Monte Titano, it’s the remarkable history that makes them stay. Its warren of medieval streets blend Renaissance, early modern and 20th-century architecture, while a trio of towers top the mountain peak. Here’s how to navigate San Marino’s layers of proud history. San Marino's medieval streets look as though they've been untouched for centuries, with steep, winding alleys and tiny piazzas. Following Bhutan's formal application for certification, an independent WHO Certification Mission is in the country from 23 August to 1 September 2026 to verify this achievement. The mission is reviewing the country's surveillance and response systems, laboratory and case-management capacity, vector control measures, policies, documentation, and field-level implementation—along with Bhutan's readiness to prevent malaria from returning. This is a defining moment in Bhutan's public health journey, marking the result of decades of hard work by health workers, communities, leaders, and partners across the country. The mission will provide recommendations to WHO on Bhutan's eligibility for malaria elimination certification while also identifying areas that need strengthening to protect this achievement. Just like the quarterback often seems to be in the spotlight, the same is true for the PCE price index. And just like there are 10 other offensive players on the field who work with the quarterback, we have many other price measures at BEA that complement the PCE price index and work together to paint the economic picture for our country. This impressive array of price measures has grown up alongside our economic accounts. Yet there was great user demand for such constant-dollar, or “real,” estimates, which are adjusted to remove the impact of prices. A House Ahead of Its Time November 4, 2024 Facebook Linkedin X.com Email The house would hardly stand out if plopped into one of the neighborhoods that surround NIST’s sprawling Gaithersburg, Maryland, campus. Its sloped driveway leads to an attached garage. Pleasant eco-friendly landscaping, unassuming green-grey siding and classic-looking windows and doors all contribute to a sense of stately suburban normalcy. Only the unusually dense array of rooftop solar panels and the scientific equipment scattered around the perimeter hint that this house might be special. Step inside, and any illusion of normality vanishes. This is, in fact, a very strange house — one humming with energy and activity despite having no flesh-and-blood occupants. This house is not haunted, but it’s also not inhabited by humans. Its residents are electrical devices run by software. Sensors measure temperature, humidity, chemicals and more. A dozen bold Afghan stallions, lashed to frenzy, collided in combat around the headless goat sprawled in the dust. These were fighting horses, giants 17 hands high, trained to kick and bite. Sweating and shouting, their turbaned riders hacked away with short whips at men and beasts alike. I plunged my horse into the battle. “ Wardar! Wardar! ” screamed the crowd. “Pick it up!” Through the billowing dust I saw my friend Mohammed Ali Hussein swoop down. Hanging from one stirrup amid the flying hoofs, he snatched the prize from the ground. His horse reared, kicking to clear an opening, but Mohammed was surrounded. He thrust the carcass into my hands. Instinctively my horse whirled. I locked the goat under my leg and galloped for the flag, a quarter of a mile down the field. “ Namani! Begeer! ” came shouts at my heels. “Grab it! Get him!” National sport befits a rugged land This was buz kashi, Afghanistan's national sport, a roughshod ancestor of polo with as many as a hundred horses on a team, a beheaded goat or calf for a ball—and almost no holds barred. pages.text: A Kelvin Wave Is Pulsing Up the West Coast. Here’s What to Expect. | National Geographic ENVIRONMENT A Pacific 'Blob' Is Pulsing Up the West Coast. Here's What's to Expect. Scientists say the Kelvin wave could be dangerous for people—and deadly for wildlife—as it travels up the California coast. Last month, around 20 homes were evacuated in Long Beach, California after heavy surf caused flooding. A blob of warm water known as a Kelvin wave is exacerbating coastal flooding caused by warmer waters, storms, and rising seas. Mario Tama, Getty Images By Ruby Mellen Published October 6, 2026 Sea levels across the west coasts of the Americas are rising after a massive bulge of water, driven by wind changes and a warmer ocean, inched its way east along the equator and along the coasts. The phenomenon, called a Kelvin wave, has officials bracing for storm surges, erosion, and transformations in marine life. Networks of satellites and buoys across the ocean have been tracking the pulse of water, which arrived on Southern California’s coast last week and will continue north. Experts say that while the wave itself isn’t especially damaging to property or infrastructure along the coast, it can worsen the damage already being inflicted by an increase in storms, climate change-driven sea-level rise, and record-high ocean temperatures, which cause water to expand. It’s also one of the major signs that the much-anticipated super El Niño born in the equatorial Pacific Ocean has made it to North and South America. LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr For 75 years, the Department of Energy's (DOE) Office of Scientific and Technical Information (OSTI) has continuously worked to increase scientific knowledge through easier access to federal research results. This dedication is evident in OSTI's deep-rooted history of creating and hosting inventive search tools and services. Prior to the digital era, OSTI's predecessor, the Atomic Energy Commission's (AEC) Technical Information Division (TID), operated one of the few federal printing plants in the United States. In 1948, TID began the production of the Nuclear Science Abstracts (NSA) journal, a world-renowned tool that provided coverage of unclassified nuclear information. Throughout its nearly 30-year tenure, NSA's quality of service to the nuclear community set a benchmark for future abstracting journals and international scientific and technical information (STI) management. OSTI entered the Internet era with the creation of the first DOE home page in 1994.
